summary: Peggy Karp proposes rules for forming ARPANET host names after feedback on her first list in RFC 226. Names would be eight characters, of the form site, dash, machine, with the site part built from the name or a standard acronym. It replaced RFC 226.

eli5.summary: A recipe for making a computer's nickname from its site and machine: a short site code, a dash, then a short machine code.

questions: host name rules site dash machine
how were arpanet host names formed
subtitle: Peggy Karp's 1971 rules for building ARPANET host names from a site code and a machine code.

tldr.problem: Earlier strawman host name lists drew comments, and the network still lacked general rules for forming host names.
tldr.mechanism: Names are 8 characters in the form site, a dash, then machine. The site part is at most 4 characters chosen by a priority list, and the machine part is at most 4 characters based on the manufacturer's model number.
tldr.outcome: The rules were subject to approval by the Network Working Group, and the list was to be maintained by the NIC with each site's technical liaison. It obsoletes RFC 226.

today: RFC 247 obsoletes RFC 226. The next RFC in this series, RFC 273, notes that no past proposal, including this one, had yet achieved acceptance.

sections.title: The Naming Rules
sections.content:
Host names are 8 characters long in the form <site>-<machine>. The site part is at most 4 characters, chosen in order: the keyword in the site name if it has not more than four characters, the standard acronym if it fits, a standard abbreviation, or the first four letters of the site name. If none is acceptable to the site, the technical liaison selects the mnemonic.

The machine part is at most 4 characters of the form manufacturer number plus designator. Examples are a 2 digit model number for an IBM 360, a 3 digit one for an IBM 370 and 4 digits for Burroughs and CDC. The designator is used when more than one machine of the same type is at a site.
sections.eli5: Pick a short code for the place, add a dash, and then add a short code for the kind of computer. If there are two of the same kind, add a letter to tell them apart.

sections.title: Special Cases and Alternates
sections.content:
Limiting the machine part to 4 characters cannot separate machines with 4 digit numbers. The author expects the NIC to handle that ad hoc. TIPs are identified as TIP rather than 316, and a host that is not permanently addressable is identified as TEST.

Alternate host names, as suggested by Jon Postel in RFC 236, should also be provided. The technical liaison selects the alternate name for his site and tells the NIC.
sections.eli5: Special machines get special codes, like TIP for the small terminal machines and TEST for ones that are only borrowed for a while.

sections.title: The Attached List and Implementation Idea
sections.content:
Attachment 1 lists network addresses with their standard names, such as address 1 as UCLA-7, address 65 as UCLA-91 and address 158 as BBNX-TEST.

Attachment 2 gives Steve Crocker's scheme: map the site into an 8-bit number S and the machine into an 8-bit number M so that S + M equals the network address. Then giving the site alone can default to the primary host at the site. For example, UCLA is X'41', which is 65, the address of UCLA-91.
sections.eli5: The paper lists every computer's number and name. A neat trick adds two small numbers, one for the place and one for the machine, to get the computer's number.

sections.title: Approval and Maintenance
sections.content: The rules and the list are subject to approval by the Network Working Group. After that, the list is to be generated and maintained by the NIC in cooperation with the technical liaison at each site, as suggested in RFC 237. Comments go to Dick Watson.
sections.eli5: Everyone had to agree first. After that, the information office keeps the list up to date with help from each site.
